criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1 (and triggers Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). The paper examines tradable raw water-resource extraction rights and agricultural irrigation water flows under Chile's 1981 Water Code, focusing on peasant farmers (campesinos) and rural indigenous communities whose irrigation/surface/groundwater rights are infringed by industrial agriculture, mining, aquaculture, real estate investors, and bulk raw-water extractors. Apart from a single passing background sentence citing UNSD national rural drinking-water statistics (p. 416), it does not study household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper WOULD satisfy Criterion 2 alone because it examines legal, administrative, and judicial governance factors under Chile's 1981 Water Code (private tradable water rights, DGA administrative formalism in regularising water rights and Water User Associations, WUA voting/membership rules, and civil court enforcement costs and delays); however, plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper still fails Criteria 1 and 4. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, c2_legal_admin_factor is 'no' because although property-right regularisation, administrative burden, WUA voting rules, and judicial enforcement are rule-type mechanisms, here they govern raw natural-resource extraction and agricultural irrigation rights rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Combines formal game-theoretic modelling with qualitative empirical evidence, including nine primary key-informant interviews/personal communications conducted in Chile in March-May 2002 (officials at DGA, DOH, INDAP, NGOs, academics, and a lawyer) and eleven documented water-right conflict cases compiled from secondary agency, academic, and press sources (Table 1), alongside secondary socioeconomic and judicial-trust statistics (Tables 2-4).
criterion_notes.c4: Outcomes reported are infringements (diversion, over-extraction, groundwater depletion, and pollution) of raw water and agricultural irrigation rights, resulting agricultural income loss and forced land sales among peasant farmers, and rational non-reporting of water-right violations to Water User Associations or courts. No household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access outcome is analysed.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (Chilean peasant farmer irrigators/campesinos and rural indigenous water-right holders, analysed at the actor-dyad and community conflict-case level), exposure (1981 Chilean Water Code institutional/enforcement regime under asymmetric wealth and power), outcome (unreported violations of raw/irrigation water rights), and study design (game-theoretic model paired with qualitative case studies and key-informant interviews) are identifiable.

study_design: Formal game-theoretic analysis combined with qualitative conflict-case illustrations and primary key-informant interviews
population_and_sample: Underprivileged raw-water users in Chile, primarily peasant farmer irrigators (campesinos; ~225,000 small producers/minifundistas nationally) and rural indigenous communities, illustrated via 11 documented water-conflict cases (Table 1) and 9 key-informant interviews
exposure: Institutional framework of Chile's 1981 Water Code water market (tradable raw water rights, DGA administrative regularisation formalism, irrigation Water User Association governance, and costly/slow civil judicial enforcement) interacting with economic and social power asymmetries
outcome: Violations (illegal diversion, over-extraction, or regularisation takeover) of peasant farmers' and indigenous communities' agricultural irrigation and raw water rights, agricultural livelihood loss, and non-reporting of infringements to WUAs or courts
rationale: Exclude under E07 (Wrong service; see Exclusion Criterion 7: 'Water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access'). Galaz (2004) uses game theory, 11 secondary conflict cases, and 9 key-informant interviews to examine why powerful actors (industrial farmers, mining companies, aquaculture firms, real estate investors, and bulk raw-water extractors) violate the raw surface/groundwater and agricultural irrigation rights of peasant farmers (campesinos) and rural indigenous communities under Chile's 1981 Water Code. Even when an urban water utility (SENDOS/ESSAT) appears in one case and in the game model, it is analysed as a bulk raw-water extractor competing with downstream agricultural irrigators, not in relation to household or community drinking-water or sanitation service delivery, connection, tariffs, or domestic access. Both under the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 wording, the study is excluded because it fails Criterion 1 (service access) and Criterion 4 (service access outcome).
